working_definition: The sender claims to have sent money to the recipient by mistake and asks for it to be returned, usually to a different number, when no genuine incoming transfer took place. Often preceded by a fake transaction confirmation SMS. Use when the sender asserts the recipient received funds. If the claim is instead that the recipient's own payment went astray, use TAX-002.

The message tells the recipient that a payment they made went to the wrong account or person and asks them to pay again, or to send funds to a new "correct" number to fix it. The focus is the recipient's own outgoing payment. If the sender claims to have mistakenly sent money to the recipient, use TAX-001.

An unsolicited message offers a job or easy income and pushes the recipient to an external link, app or chat group to apply, with no sign that the recipient applied for anything. Use when the link is the main hook and no fee has been requested yet. If a fee appears, prefer the matching advance fee subtype.

The message claims the recipient has been shortlisted, selected or invited to interview for a role, typically one they never applied for or with vague employer details, to build trust ahead of a later request. Use when no payment is requested in the message itself. If a fee is requested, use TAX-005 or TAX-008.

The recipient is told to pay a registration, application or booking fee to secure an interview slot or place in a recruitment exercise. The payment is framed as the cost of being considered for the job. If the payment is framed as onboarding after selection, use TAX-008.

An offer of work abroad (commonly in the Gulf, Europe or North America) is made conditional on paying an unverified agent for placement, visa processing, medical checks, flights or travel documents. Use when the destination job is overseas and the agent requests payment before departure.

The recipient is offered paid online tasks such as liking videos, rating products or simple data entry, then asked to pay to activate an account, unlock a higher earning tier or withdraw accumulated earnings. Small early payouts are often used to build trust before larger deposits are demanded.

After a supposed job offer, the recipient is told to pay for mandatory orientation, training, uniforms, medical tests or onboarding materials before starting work. The payment is framed as a step after selection. If it is framed as the cost of getting an interview, use TAX-005.

A message demands school fees, levies or other charges supposedly on behalf of a school, through channels that cannot be verified as official (unknown number, personal account, no reference to the school's usual paybill). Use when the demand itself is suspect but there is no explicit claim that the payment details have changed. For a stated change of account, use TAX-049.

The sender poses as a student, relative or school staff member and urgently asks for money for an unexpected school expense, such as an exam fee, a trip, a threatened suspension or an incident at school. The framing is a personal emergency rather than an institutional fee demand (TAX-009).

The recipient is told that a parcel, package or consignment they were not expecting, often from abroad or from an unnamed "friend", is held at customs, an airport or a courier and requires payment of clearance, duty or release fees. Use when there is no prior purchase. For goods bought through a marketplace, use TAX-038.

The message tells the recipient to send money to a specific number, till or account with little or no explanation or pretext. This is a fallback label. Use it only when the message cannot be reliably mapped to any more specific subtype, and never when a recognisable pretext is present.

A request for urgent money arrives from a known contact's genuine messaging or social media account that has been taken over. The message relies on the recipient trusting the familiar account and often cites an emergency or a temporary inability to talk. If the sender instead claims to be a known person writing from a new number, use TAX-047.

A message claiming to be from a landlord, caretaker or property agent tells tenants that rent should now be paid to a new paybill, till or account number. The key cue is an announced change of payment details.

A message styled as a routine rent reminder insists that payment go only to a specified number or account and often warns tenants against using other channels, such as paying at the office. Use when exclusivity is stressed without an explicit announcement of changed details. For an announced change, use TAX-014.

The message claims the recipient's mobile money account has been or will be suspended, blocked or limited and urges them to call a number, follow a link, dial a code or share their PIN or personal details to restore it. Use for mobile money wallets. For bank accounts, use TAX-019.

The sender poses as customer care for a bank, telco or digital platform and sends a link to "verify", "secure" or "fix" the recipient's account, sometimes referring to a complaint or call the recipient never made. The key cue is the support agent persona. If the request is framed as a routine compliance update without that persona, use TAX-020.

The recipient is told they have earned a mobile money bonus, cashback or loyalty reward and must follow a link, dial a code, pay a small fee or share details to claim it. Use when the reward is tied to a mobile money service. For airtime or data rewards, use TAX-033.

The message claims the recipient's bank account has been frozen, flagged or restricted over suspicious activity or missing information and directs them to a link or number to unlock it, typically to capture login credentials or one time codes. For mobile money wallets, use TAX-016.

The message asks the recipient to update their KYC (Know Your Customer) details, such as ID number, date of birth or PIN, by a deadline to avoid deactivation, via a link or by replying. It is framed as routine regulatory compliance rather than as a response to suspicious activity (TAX-016, TAX-019) or as contact from a support agent (TAX-017).

The message claims that a transfer to or from the recipient is pending or on hold and needs confirmation, a code, a login or a release fee before it can complete. Use when the hook is a specific transaction awaiting action.

The message claims the recipient's ATM, debit or credit card needs verification, reactivation or an upgrade and asks for the card number, PIN, CVV or a one time code. Use when the request centres on card details rather than account login.

The recipient is offered or told they have been approved for a loan, then asked to pay a processing, insurance, credit bureau clearance or other fee before the money is disbursed. Often targets people who have struggled to get credit elsewhere.

A rental listing, often priced below the market rate, comes with a demand for a deposit, booking fee or viewing fee before the property can be seen. The supposed landlord or agent typically has excuses for being unavailable in person.

A message to residents of a building, estate or gated community, claiming to come from management, a residents' association or a caretaker, asks for contributions toward repairs, security, water or cleaning to an unofficial account.

A message claiming to be from an electricity, water or other utility provider threatens imminent disconnection over unpaid bills and demands immediate payment to a specified number or through a link. The key cue is time pressure tied to loss of service.

The message impersonates the tax authority and says the recipient is owed a tax refund, directing them to a link or form that collects login credentials, tax PIN, ID or banking details. The aim is data capture rather than an upfront payment.

The message impersonates a government agency, court, police or traffic authority and demands payment of a fine, penalty or arrears to avoid arrest, prosecution or licence suspension. Use when the core request is direct payment. If the core request is clicking a link to submit details, use TAX-027 or TAX-029.

The message claims a business permit, driving licence, passport or similar document is expiring or invalid and directs the recipient to a link or unofficial agent to renew it, capturing personal details or fees.
The message offers a government grant, relief payment, stipend or empowerment fund, often aimed at youth, women or farmers, conditional on registering through a link or paying a processing fee.
The message claims the recipient's national or digital ID registration needs updating or verifying and asks for their ID number, personal details, photos or a fee, through a link or by reply.

The message says the recipient has won a lottery, raffle or promotion they never entered and must pay a clearance, tax or processing fee to receive cash winnings. For a physical prize with a delivery fee, use TAX-035.

The message offers free airtime, data bundles or other telco bonuses through a link or a dialling code, aiming to capture personal details, credentials or subscriptions to premium services. For mobile money rewards, use TAX-018.

The recipient is invited to complete a short survey, often using a familiar brand, in exchange for cash, airtime or a prize. The survey leads to a form that collects personal or payment details, or to a request for a small fee.

The message says the recipient has won a physical item such as a phone, TV or gas cylinder in a giveaway and must pay a delivery, shipping or registration fee to receive it. For cash prizes, use TAX-032. For goods the recipient actually bought, use TAX-038.

The message warns that loyalty points with a supermarket, airline, telco or bank are about to expire and urges redemption through a link that collects credentials or card details. The key cue is urgency around points the recipient supposedly already holds, as opposed to a newly awarded bonus (TAX-018).

A seller on an online marketplace, social media page or classifieds site asks for a deposit or full payment to "reserve" or "hold" an item before the buyer can see or inspect it, then typically stops responding.

After a marketplace purchase or agreed sale, the buyer is told the item is with a courier or transporter and that a release, insurance or clearance fee must be paid before delivery. Use when a purchase preceded the message. For unexpected parcels, use TAX-011.

A supposed buyer claims to have overpaid, often backed by a fake transaction message or a payment that can be reversed, and asks the seller to refund the excess before the original payment clears or is reversed.

The other party pushes to move the transaction off the official platform to a fake escrow, payment protection or third party service, through a link or account they control. The key cue is the push away from the platform's own payment system.

The buyer is told the goods are held at a warehouse, depot or courier and that daily storage or demurrage charges are building up, creating pressure to pay quickly. Use when the fee is framed as a growing, time based charge. For a single release fee, use TAX-038.

The message offers an investment with high, fixed or risk free returns over a short period (for example "double your money in 7 days"), often backed by testimonials or referral rewards that suggest a pyramid or Ponzi structure.

The message impersonates a crypto exchange, wallet provider or trading platform and asks the recipient to verify, sync or unlock their wallet or account by entering a seed phrase, private key, password or one time code.
The recipient is invited to pay a membership or subscription fee to join a VIP trading signals group, forex or crypto mentorship, or an account management service that promises profitable trades.

The message offers investment in a farming venture, such as fruit trees, poultry, livestock, greenhouses or farmland, with unrealistic fixed returns or guaranteed buyback of produce. Use instead of TAX-042 when the pitch is specifically agricultural.

The message claims the recipient's investment profits, dividends or withdrawal are ready but blocked until they pay a tax, upgrade, verification or release fee. Use when the hook is unlocking existing returns rather than making a new investment.

The sender claims to be a known relative or friend writing from a new or borrowed number ("this is my new number") and urgently asks for money. If the message comes from the contact's own hijacked account, use TAX-013.

The sender claims a relative or friend has been admitted to hospital or been in an accident and urgently asks for money for treatment, a deposit or discharge, often discouraging the recipient from calling to check.

The message claims a school's fee account, paybill or bank details have changed and directs parents or guardians to pay to the new details. The key cue is an announced change of payment details. For a suspect fee demand with no such change, use TAX-009.

The message asks for donations to a charity, church, disaster relief effort, medical fundraiser or funeral using an unverified or impersonated identity, and directs funds to a personal number or account.

The sender, often posing as a contact, platform or support agent, asks the recipient to share a verification code supposedly "sent by mistake". The code is then used to take over the recipient's messaging, social media or financial account.
The message offers a scholarship, bursary or study abroad sponsorship conditional on paying an application, processing or administration fee.
The message offers early or guaranteed access to national exam results through a link, a premium SMS code or a payment, aiming to collect fees or personal details from students and parents.
The message promises admission or a guaranteed place at a school, college or university, conditional on paying an admission deposit or confirmation fee through unofficial channels.
The message claims the recipient's health, motor or life insurance policy is inactive or about to lapse and must be activated or renewed urgently by paying to a specified number or through a link.

The message says the recipient is eligible for a medical insurance refund or reimbursement and directs them to a link or form that collects personal, banking or login details. The aim is data capture rather than an upfront payment.
